clinicalPearls: Results from a lesion of the ventral caudal pons, usually ischaemic, in the territory of paramedian and short circumferential branches of the basilar artery
Combines ipsilateral facial (seventh nerve) and abducens (sixth nerve) palsies with contralateral hemiparesis
The facial weakness is of lower motor neurone type, affecting the whole ipsilateral face including the forehead
The sixth nerve palsy causes failure of ipsilateral eye abduction and horizontal diplopia
Contralateral limb weakness reflects involvement of the corticospinal fibres in the basis pontis before they decussate
It is a lower alternating hemiplegia, contrasting with the midbrain (Weber) upper alternating hemiplegia
Adjacent involvement of horizontal gaze structures may add a gaze palsy, overlapping with Foville syndrome
reference.pathophysiology: Millard-Gubler syndrome follows a lesion of the ventral caudal pons supplied by paramedian and short circumferential branches of the basilar artery. The infarct or haemorrhage damages the intrapontine fascicles of the facial and abducens nerves as they course towards their exit, producing ipsilateral lower motor neurone facial weakness and a lateral rectus palsy, together with the descending corticospinal fibres in the basis pontis, producing contralateral hemiparesis with facial sparing on the weak side. Because the cranial nerve deficits are ipsilateral and the limb weakness contralateral, the picture is that of a caudal alternating hemiplegia; extension towards the paramedian pontine reticular formation can add an ipsilateral horizontal gaze palsy.
additionalDifferentials: Locked-in syndrome from extensive ventral pontine infarction
Cerebellopontine angle lesion affecting the facial and abducens nerves
Basilar artery thrombosis with evolving brainstem signs
additionalInvestigations: Diffusion-weighted MRI of the pons to confirm a ventral caudal pontine lesion
MR or CT angiography of the basilar artery and posterior circulation
Assessment of facial nerve function distinguishing upper from lower motor neurone weakness
Ocular motility testing for abduction deficit and horizontal gaze
Cardiovascular and stroke risk workup including ECG and metabolic profiling
Vessel wall imaging where basilar atherosclerosis or dissection is suspected
redFlags: Progressive drowsiness or quadriparesis suggesting evolving basilar thrombosis
Bilateral pontine signs raising the possibility of a locked-in state
Rapidly worsening deficit indicating an expanding pontine haemorrhage
New respiratory or swallowing compromise from brainstem extension
reference.prognosis: Isolated small ventral pontine infarcts may show useful recovery of limb power and facial function, but larger lesions or those heralding basilar thrombosis carry a poor prognosis with risk of progression to a locked-in state.
pitfalls: Mistaking the lower motor neurone facial palsy for a peripheral Bell palsy in isolation
Overlooking the contralateral hemiparesis and missing the brainstem localisation
Failing to recognise an evolving basilar occlusion behind apparently limited signs
Confusing an added gaze palsy with a hemispheric gaze deviation
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Treat the acute pontine infarct as a stroke, giving intravenous thrombolysis within the therapeutic window and considering endovascular thrombectomy for basilar artery occlusion
Admit to a stroke unit and monitor closely for progression to basilar thrombosis or a locked-in state
Institute secondary prevention with antiplatelet therapy, a statin and control of blood pressure and other vascular risk factors, using anticoagulation if a cardioembolic source is found
Protect the eye affected by facial weakness with lubricants and lid taping, and manage horizontal diplopia with occlusion or prisms
Provide multidisciplinary rehabilitation with physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech and language therapy
Investigate and address the underlying cause, such as basilar atherosclerosis or arterial dissection
